transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, yes, nice to meet you too. Thank you so much for fitting me in. 

Well, as to what brings me in... it's a bit embarrassing to admit at my age, honestly. I'm sixty, and I've been a high school teacher for decades—mostly history, some government classes—so you would really think I'd have mastered the art of sitting through a long meeting by now. But I just... I keep getting up. That's the main thing. I keep getting up in situations where everyone else is perfectly content being seated, and it's starting to become a real issue for me. 

Like, if I'm in a faculty meeting, everyone else is just sitting there, listening to the principal or taking notes, but I will suddenly feel like I absolutely have to stand. I'll make up little excuses to myself, you know? I'll think, "Oh, I need to refill my coffee right now," even if my cup is still half full, or I'll get up to check a stack of handouts on the back table, or I'll just walk to the back of the room and stand by the door, even though nothing is really urgent at all. 

And it’s not just at school, it’s in my personal life too. At dinner! My husband and I will be eating, maybe we even have friends over for a nice meal, and everyone is sitting and chatting, but I'll just pop up out of my chair. I'll go check the oven, or look for a different serving spoon, or just stand by the kitchen island for a few minutes. My husband actually joked the other night that I’m like a jack-in-the-box, which, well, it made me laugh at first, but then it made me realize how much I'm actually doing it. It makes other people feel rushed or distracted, I think. I just can't seem to stay planted in my seat when I'm supposed to, and I really don't understand why I can't just sit through a meal or a meeting like a normal adult. So, that's why I'm here.
When you’re sitting and feel you have to get up, do you also get an uncomfortable feeling in your legs that eases when you stand or walk?

No, no, it's not like that. I don't have any sort of physical ache or tingling or anything creepy-crawly like that. My legs themselves feel completely fine. There's no pain, no discomfort in the muscles or the joints or anything of that nature. It's more just... well, it's this overwhelming sense that I shouldn't be sitting anymore. Like the chair is suddenly just the wrong place to be. 

I'll just be sitting there, and my legs are perfectly comfortable, but my brain is just saying, "Okay, time to get up now, let's go." It's almost like a spring uncoiling, but not in a physical or painful way, if that makes sense? Just a sudden, absolute necessity to be vertical. Like yesterday, I was grading papers at the kitchen table—just AP History essays, which take forever, honestly, because the kids write these sprawling paragraphs and you really have to focus to follow their arguments—and my legs were totally fine, just resting on the rung of the stool. But I just had to stand up. I ended up taking the whole stack of rubrics and papers over to the island to grade standing up for the next twenty minutes. 

I didn't feel any physical relief in my legs when I stood, because they didn't hurt or feel restless to begin with, but I just felt... better, overall, being up. Like I was finally doing what I was supposed to be doing. So, no, definitely no uncomfortable feeling in my legs specifically. It's not a physical ache at all.
When you're expected to stay seated, do you find your mind wandering so much that getting up helps you refocus?

Well, no, I wouldn't say it's about refocusing, exactly. It's not like I'm sitting there and my mind is drifting off to, oh, I don't know, what I'm going to make for dinner or my grocery list or wondering if I left the porch light on. I mean, sure, everyone's mind wanders a bit, especially during those long professional development days where they bring in some consultant who hasn't been in a classroom since 1995 to tell us how to engage teenagers. But it's not that I'm losing my train of thought and standing up brings it back. 

It's actually almost the opposite? Like, I can be completely focused on what's happening. I could be totally engrossed in a student's presentation on the Industrial Revolution, or right in the middle of a really good conversation with my husband about our weekend plans, and I still just have to get up. My brain is right there in the moment, fully engaged, but my body just... rebels against the chair. 

I remember last week, we had a faculty meeting about the new grading software, which, let me tell you, is a nightmare to navigate, but I was actually really trying to pay attention because I needed to know how to input my midterm grades. I was taking notes, I was following along on my laptop, I was completely dialed in. And yet, I still found myself standing up and migrating to the back of the library. I didn't stand up to concentrate better on the software demonstration; I just stood up because I couldn't sit anymore. And honestly, sometimes getting up actually distracts me more because then I have to think of a reason why I'm standing, like pretending to look at the bulletin board, instead of just focusing on the meeting. So, no, I don't think it's a matter of my mind wandering and needing to reset my focus. It's just... the sitting itself that I can't seem to tolerate for very long.
When you have to get up, do you feel an inner restlessness?

Well, an inner restlessness... I suppose that's one way to put it, though I'm not entirely sure if "restlessness" captures the whole picture, or maybe it captures it too perfectly? It's hard to explain without sounding a bit dramatic. But yes, I suppose there is this... this buzzing feeling inside. It’s not physical, like I said about my legs, but it's like my engine is just idling too high. 

I remember trying to explain this to my sister once—she’s a retired librarian, very calm, very sedate, could sit in a wingback chair with a cup of tea for six hours straight and not twitch once. I told her it feels like I have a motor running inside me that I can’t quite shut off. Even when I’m sitting, even when I’m perfectly comfortable, there’s this low-level hum of energy that just builds and builds. It’s like when you’re waiting for water to boil, and you see those little bubbles starting at the bottom of the pot, and you know it’s about to roil over. That’s what it feels like inside my chest or my head, just this constant, low-grade need for motion. 

It’s exhausting sometimes, to be honest. Like last weekend, I was sitting on the patio, beautiful weather, a lovely breeze, reading a biography of Eleanor Roosevelt—fascinating woman, really, the amount of energy she had was astounding—and I should have been perfectly relaxed. But inside, I just felt this... this tightness. This urge to do something, anything, other than just sit there. I ended up getting up to deadhead the petunias, then I swept the porch, then I went inside to reorganize the Tupperware drawer, all because I couldn't just sit with that feeling. So, yes, I suppose "inner restlessness" is a good way to describe it, though it feels more like an internal pressure that just demands I get moving.
During these times, do you feel unusually euphoric or excessively upbeat?

No, no, definitely not. It's not a happy feeling at all. I wouldn't call it euphoric or upbeat in the slightest. It's actually quite the opposite, really. It's more of an annoyance, a frustration that I can't just be still like everyone else seems to be able to do. 

I mean, when I'm up and moving because of that internal pressure, I'm not doing it with a spring in my step or a song in my heart. I'm not whistling while I work, like some cheerful cartoon character. Take that time I was reorganizing the Tupperware drawer—I wasn't thrilled to be doing it. I was actually quite irritated because I *wanted* to be sitting on the patio reading about Eleanor Roosevelt. I *wanted* to be relaxing. But I was practically throwing the plastic lids around because I was just so aggravated by this need to be doing something. 

My husband, bless him, sometimes he’ll see me pacing around the living room during a movie—we were trying to watch that new historical drama on PBS last night, beautifully costumed, really quite stunning, but I couldn't stay on the sofa for more than twenty minutes—and he'll ask if I'm excited about something. And I have to tell him, no, I'm not excited, I'm just... compelled. It's not a joyful energy. It's just a relentless one. So, no, there's no euphoria involved at all. Just a lot of sighing and wishing I could just sit still and enjoy a quiet moment without my body deciding it's time to run a marathon.
When this urge to get up happens, do you feel anxious?

Anxious? Well... I suppose it depends on how you define anxious, doesn't it? I mean, I'm not sitting there worrying about, oh, whether I left the stove on, or if my students are going to fail their state exams—though, frankly, with the way the curriculum is structured these days, that's a valid concern for any teacher. But it's not a fearful anxiety. It's not like my heart is pounding because I'm scared of something or because I'm having a panic attack. I've had colleagues who get panic attacks, and it sounds just awful, but this isn't that.

But, on the other hand, if you mean anxious as in... keyed up, or agitated? Then maybe yes. Because when I can't get up, when I'm forced to just sit there and endure that buzzing feeling I told you about, I do start to feel a bit frantic. Like, I remember being at my niece's graduation ceremony last spring. Oh, it was lovely, she looked beautiful, valedictorian and everything, but the ceremony was *three hours long*. Three hours! Sitting on those hard metal folding chairs in a stuffy gymnasium. And by the second hour, when they were only halfway through the M's, I was practically crawling out of my skin. I wasn't worried or scared, but I was so incredibly tense and agitated that I felt like I was going to scream if I couldn't stand up and stretch my legs. I kept crossing and uncrossing my ankles, shifting my weight, checking my watch every two minutes. 

My sister kept giving me these side-eyes, you know the look, the "stop fidgeting, you're embarrassing me" look. And that made me feel a little stressed, I suppose, because I knew I was being disruptive, but I just couldn't help it. The longer I had to suppress the urge to move, the more unbearable it became. So, it's not a psychological anxiety, where my mind is racing with worries. It's more of a physical distress, a desperate need for release. I don't know if that's what you mean by anxious, but that's the closest I can get to describing it. It's just this overwhelming, physical imperative to move, and when I can't, it's sheer torture.
Did this problem start after you began a new medication or changed the dose of one?

No, no, nothing like that. I haven't started any new medications recently, nor have I changed the dose of anything I'm currently taking. I mean, I take a daily multivitamin, and calcium for my bones—you know, at my age, you really have to start thinking about osteoporosis, especially since my mother had it quite terribly in her later years, shrinking down to practically nothing, poor thing. And I take a little something for my blood pressure, just a very low dose that Dr. Evans prescribed about five years ago, but that's been perfectly stable. 

I haven't tweaked a thing. I'm very particular about following instructions when it comes to medications. I have one of those little pill organizers, the ones with the days of the week printed on them in big letters? Sunday through Saturday. I keep it right next to the coffee maker so I don't forget. So, no, it's definitely not a medication issue. This feeling, this... constant motor running, it's not a new development tied to a pill. It's just... well, it's just how I've been. It's not a side effect of anything I'm swallowing in the morning with my orange juice, I can assure you of that.
Have you been needing much less sleep than usual?

Less sleep? Oh, no, not at all. I mean, I certainly wouldn't say I *need* less sleep. If anything, I wish I could get more of it! I still aim for my solid eight hours every single night. I'm quite disciplined about it, really. I try to be in bed by 10:00 PM, lights out by 10:30 PM after I've read a chapter or two of whatever biography I'm currently absorbed in—right now it's a fascinating one on Abigail Adams, she really was quite ahead of her time, you know. 

But my sleep hasn't changed. I still feel tired at the end of the day, just like anyone else. Teaching teenagers all day takes it out of you, let me tell you! By the time I've graded the last essay and prepped the lesson plan for the next morning, I am more than ready to put my head on the pillow. It's not like I'm staying up until three in the morning scrubbing the baseboards or feeling like I could run a marathon. I don't have that kind of... limitless energy where I just don't feel the need to rest. 

Now, actually *falling* asleep, well, sometimes that takes a minute because my mind might still be going over the events of the day, or I might be tossing and turning a bit because my legs feel restless—like they haven't gotten the memo that it's time to power down. But the *need* for sleep? Oh, yes, that is very much still there. If I don't get my eight hours, I am absolutely dragging the next day in the classroom, and you simply cannot be sluggish when you're trying to explain the intricacies of the American Revolution to thirty 11th graders. They will eat you alive! So, no, my sleep requirements haven't decreased in the slightest. I need every minute of rest I can get.
Has anyone told you that your behavior or speech becomes disorganized or hard to follow?

Disorganized? Hard to follow? Well... I don't think so. I mean, certainly not in a way that anyone has ever felt the need to point out to me as a problem. As a teacher, you have to be organized in your speech, don't you? You have to be able to lay out a lesson plan clearly—first we discuss the causes, then the major battles, then the aftermath. If you're disorganized, the students just check out immediately. They'll start looking at their phones under the desks, or staring out the window, and you've lost them entirely. 

Now, do I sometimes go off on a tangent? Oh, absolutely. I'll be talking about the Boston Tea Party, and then suddenly I'm reminded of this fascinating article I read about the history of tea smuggling in the 18th century, and how it impacted the East India Company, and before I know it, I've spent five minutes talking about maritime trade routes instead of the Sons of Liberty. But I always bring it back around! It's just... I get enthusiastic, you know? There's so much interesting context, and I want them to see the whole picture, not just memorize a list of dates. 

My husband, Arthur—bless him—he sometimes jokes that I take the scenic route when I'm telling a story. Like the other day, I was trying to tell him about a disagreement two of my colleagues were having in the staff room over the new grading policy, and I started explaining the background of the policy, and then how the principal introduced it at the last faculty meeting, and what she was wearing—she had this awful mustard yellow scarf on, I don't know who told her that was her color—and Arthur just sort of chuckled and said, "Darling, I think we've lost the plot." But he was just teasing. It wasn't that I wasn't making sense, I was just giving him all the details! 

So, no, no one has ever told me my speech is actually disorganized or impossible to follow. I might talk a lot, and I might weave a few different threads together, but it all makes sense in the end. I'm not speaking gibberish or jumping from one completely unrelated thought to another without any connection. It's just a very... detailed way of communicating, I suppose.
When you feel compelled to stand up, does it ever seem like some outside force is making you move?

An outside force? Oh, heavens, no. Nothing like that. It's not as though I'm being puppeted on strings or... or possessed by some sort of spirit, if that's what you're asking! It's entirely me. It's completely internal. 

It's just this... this build-up of energy, I suppose you could say. It comes from right inside my own bones. Like just last week, we had this dreadful professional development seminar—two solid hours on the new standardized testing protocols, and they had us sitting in those awful, rigid plastic folding chairs in the gymnasium. You know the ones, they absolutely murder your lower back. And about forty-five minutes in, my legs just started to feel... fizzy. That's really the best word for it. Fizzy, like there was carbonation right under my skin. 

And my own brain was just telling me, "You need to stand up, you need to stretch your calves right this very second or you are going to simply burst." It's my own body demanding it. There's no mysterious entity pulling the levers or forcing me out of the chair, it's just my own absolute inability to stay glued to a seat for hours on end without getting terribly uncomfortable. 

I mean, even at home, Arthur and I were watching a documentary on the Apollo missions the other night—fascinating stuff, really, the engineering involved is just staggering when you think about the technology they had in the sixties—and even in my own perfectly comfortable recliner in my own living room, I eventually had to get up and pace behind the sofa for a bit while we watched. Arthur didn't mind, he's used to it by now, but it was just me wanting to move. Not some invisible hand pushing me up. So, no, definitely no outside forces at work here. Just my own restless self.

But I was practically throwing the plastic lids around because I was just so aggravated by this need to be doing something. 

My husband, bless him, sometimes he’ll see me pacing around the living room during a movie—we were trying to watch that new historical drama on PBS last night, beautifully costumed, really quite stunning, but I couldn't stay on the sofa for more than twenty minutes—and he'll ask if I'm excited about something. And I have to tell him, no, I'm not excited, I'm just... compelled. It's not a joyful energy. It's just a relentless one. So, no, there's no euphoria involved at all. Just a lot of sighing and wishing I could just sit still and enjoy a quiet moment without my body deciding it's time to run a marathon.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the restlessness occurs specifically during anxiety or panic, to distinguish an anxiety disorder from bipolar mania or catatonic excitement.
doctor.question: When this urge to get up happens, do you feel anxious?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of anxiety to explore differential diagnoses, which is not covered by my ADHD symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Anxious? Well... I suppose it depends on how you define anxious, doesn't it? I mean, I'm not sitting there worrying about, oh, whether I left the stove on, or if my students are going to fail their state exams—though, frankly, with the way the curriculum is structured these days, that's a valid concern for any teacher. But it's not a fearful anxiety. It's not like my heart is pounding because I'm scared of something or because I'm having a panic attack. I've had colleagues who get panic attacks, and it sounds just awful, but this isn't that.

But, on the other hand, if you mean anxious as in... keyed up, or agitated? Then maybe yes. Because when I can't get up, when I'm forced to just sit there and endure that buzzing feeling I told you about, I do start to feel a bit frantic. Like, I remember being at my niece's graduation ceremony last spring. Oh, it was lovely, she looked beautiful, valedictorian and everything, but the ceremony was *three hours long*. Three hours! Sitting on those hard metal folding chairs in a stuffy gymnasium. And by the second hour, when they were only halfway through the M's, I was practically crawling out of my skin. I wasn't worried or scared, but I was so incredibly tense and agitated that I felt like I was going to scream if I couldn't stand up and stretch my legs. I kept crossing and uncrossing my ankles, shifting my weight, checking my watch every two minutes. 

My sister kept giving me these side-eyes, you know the look, the "stop fidgeting, you're embarrassing me" look. And that made me feel a little stressed, I suppose, because I knew I was being disruptive, but I just couldn't help it. The longer I had to suppress the urge to move, the more unbearable it became. So, it's not a psychological anxiety, where my mind is racing with worries. It's more of a physical distress, a desperate need for release. I don't know if that's what you mean by anxious, but that's the closest I can get to describing it. It's just this overwhelming, physical imperative to move, and when I can't, it's sheer torture.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the restlessness began after starting or changing a medication, which would strongly support akathisia/anxiety over bipolar disorder or catatonia.
doctor.question: Did this problem start after you began a new medication or changed the dose of one?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the symptoms started after beginning or changing a medication to rule out medication-induced akathisia or side effects. My symptom profile does not contain information about medications.

patient.answer:
No, no, nothing like that. I haven't started any new medications recently, nor have I changed the dose of anything I'm currently taking. I mean, I take a daily multivitamin, and calcium for my bones—you know, at my age, you really have to start thinking about osteoporosis, especially since my mother had it quite terribly in her later years, shrinking down to practically nothing, poor thing. And I take a little something for my blood pressure, just a very low dose that Dr. Evans prescribed about five years ago, but that's been perfectly stable. 

I haven't tweaked a thing. I'm very particular about following instructions when it comes to medications. I have one of those little pill organizers, the ones with the days of the week printed on them in big letters? Sunday through Saturday. I keep it right next to the coffee maker so I don't forget. So, no, it's definitely not a medication issue. This feeling, this... constant motor running, it's not a new development tied to a pill. It's just... well, it's just how I've been. It's not a side effect of anything I'm swallowing in the morning with my orange juice, I can assure you of that.

doctor.intent: Differentiate psychomotor agitation from mania or catatonic excitement by assessing whether she has had a decreased need for sleep.
doctor.question: Have you been needing much less sleep than usual?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a decreased need for sleep, which is a symptom of mania/hypomania to rule out bipolar disorder. This is not covered by the patient's ADHD symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Less sleep? Oh, no, not at all. I mean, I certainly wouldn't say I *need* less sleep. If anything, I wish I could get more of it! I still aim for my solid eight hours every single night. I'm quite disciplined about it, really. I try to be in bed by 10:00 PM, lights out by 10:30 PM after I've read a chapter or two of whatever biography I'm currently absorbed in—right now it's a fascinating one on Abigail Adams, she really was quite ahead of her time, you know. 

But my sleep hasn't changed. I still feel tired at the end of the day, just like anyone else. Teaching teenagers all day takes it out of you, let me tell you! By the time I've graded the last essay and prepped the lesson plan for the next morning, I am more than ready to put my head on the pillow. It's not like I'm staying up until three in the morning scrubbing the baseboards or feeling like I could run a marathon. I don't have that kind of... limitless energy where I just don't feel the need to rest. 

Now, actually *falling* asleep, well, sometimes that takes a minute because my mind might still be going over the events of the day, or I might be tossing and turning a bit because my legs feel restless—like they haven't gotten the memo that it's time to power down. But the *need* for sleep? Oh, yes, that is very much still there. If I don't get my eight hours, I am absolutely dragging the next day in the classroom, and you simply cannot be sluggish when you're trying to explain the intricacies of the American Revolution to thirty 11th graders. They will eat you alive! So, no, my sleep requirements haven't decreased in the slightest. I need every minute of rest I can get.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the restlessness is accompanied by psychotic disorganization/catatonic features, which would help distinguish schizophrenia from anxiety or bipolar spectrum illness.
doctor.question: Has anyone told you that your behavior or speech becomes disorganized or hard to follow?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about disorganized behavior or speech, which are symptoms of psychosis or mania, not covered in my ADHD symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Disorganized? Hard to follow? Well... I don't think so. I mean, certainly not in a way that anyone has ever felt the need to point out to me as a problem. As a teacher, you have to be organized in your speech, don't you? You have to be able to lay out a lesson plan clearly—first we discuss the causes, then the major battles, then the aftermath. If you're disorganized, the students just check out immediately. They'll start looking at their phones under the desks, or staring out the window, and you've lost them entirely. 

Now, do I sometimes go off on a tangent? Oh, absolutely. I'll be talking about the Boston Tea Party, and then suddenly I'm reminded of this fascinating article I read about the history of tea smuggling in the 18th century, and how it impacted the East India Company, and before I know it, I've spent five minutes talking about maritime trade routes instead of the Sons of Liberty. But I always bring it back around! It's just... I get enthusiastic, you know? There's so much interesting context, and I want them to see the whole picture, not just memorize a list of dates. 

My husband, Arthur—bless him—he sometimes jokes that I take the scenic route when I'm telling a story. Like the other day, I was trying to tell him about a disagreement two of my colleagues were having in the staff room over the new grading policy, and I started explaining the background of the policy, and then how the principal introduced it at the last faculty meeting, and what she was wearing—she had this awful mustard yellow scarf on, I don't know who told her that was her color—and Arthur just sort of chuckled and said, "Darling, I think we've lost the plot." But he was just teasing. It wasn't that I wasn't making sense, I was just giving him all the details! 

So, no, no one has ever told me my speech is actually disorganized or impossible to follow. I might talk a lot, and I might weave a few different threads together, but it all makes sense in the end. I'm not speaking gibberish or jumping from one completely unrelated thought to another without any connection. It's just a very... detailed way of communicating, I suppose.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the urge to move is driven by psychosis, especially passivity experiences or external control, which would separate catatonic schizophrenia from anxiety or bipolar-spectrum agitation.
doctor.question: When you feel compelled to stand up, does it ever seem like some outside force is making you move?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about delusions of control or passivity experiences (feeling like an outside force is controlling movements), which is a psychotic symptom not covered by the ADHD symptom profile.

patient.answer:
An outside force? Oh, heavens, no. Nothing like that. It's not as though I'm being puppeted on strings or... or possessed by some sort of spirit, if that's what you're asking! It's entirely me. It's completely internal. 

It's just this... this build-up of energy, I suppose you could say. It comes from right inside my own bones. Like just last week, we had this dreadful professional development seminar—two solid hours on the new standardized testing protocols, and they had us sitting in those awful, rigid plastic folding chairs in the gymnasium. You know the ones, they absolutely murder your lower back. And about forty-five minutes in, my legs just started to feel... fizzy. That's really the best word for it. Fizzy, like there was carbonation right under my skin. 

And my own brain was just telling me, "You need to stand up, you need to stretch your calves right this very second or you are going to simply burst." It's my own body demanding it. There's no mysterious entity pulling the levers or forcing me out of the chair, it's just my own absolute inability to stay glued to a seat for hours on end without getting terribly uncomfortable. 

I mean, even at home, Arthur and I were watching a documentary on the Apollo missions the other night—fascinating stuff, really, the engineering involved is just staggering when you think about the technology they had in the sixties—and even in my own perfectly comfortable recliner in my own living room, I eventually had to get up and pace behind the sofa for a bit while we watched. Arthur didn't mind, he's used to it by now, but it was just me wanting to move. Not some invisible hand pushing me up. So, no, definitely no outside forces at work here. Just my own restless self.

inference.note: Denied euphoria/decreased need for sleep (argues against F31.9), denied disorganization/passivity phenomena (argues against F20.2), and symptoms are a chronic internal restlessness/compelled need to move without medication change, leaving anxiety-spectrum/akathisia-like restlessness best captured by F41.9 among prior options.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking care today
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a persistent internal sense of being keyed up/agitated with a compelling need to stand, pace, or move, causing social and situational impairment. Interview evidence argues against restless legs syndrome (no leg discomfort relieved by movement), mania/hypomania (no euphoria, no decreased need for sleep, no disorganization), psychosis/passivity phenomena (no outside force), and medication-induced akathisia (no recent medication change). Given the limited ICD-10 candidate set, the presentation is best captured as an unspecified anxiety/agitation condition.
